newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - OH WHAT A RELIEF IT IS.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - OH WHAT A RELIEF IT IS.

text.p: After struggling to digest $38.0 billion in supply this week, U.S. Treasuries should breath a heavy sigh of relief on Friday and set their sights higher, analysts said.

The Treasury's quarterly refunding of new securities had a relatively warm reception this week. And analysts said the idle bulls may mobilize in distribution trade before nervousness over next week's crucial retail sales and inflation numbers sets in.
"Part of the Friday trade would be the bulls coming out of the woodwork again if they feel that the long bond is under control," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.

Stiles said bond market participants appeared to be in a pause phase after last Friday's huge selloff and ahead of this week's Treasury auction. But after the supply jitters fade, short-term buying is likely to emerge, he said.
The market may attempt to test the September T-bond contract's 20-day moving average of 114-29/32, he added.

Concluding its quarterly refunding effort, the Treasury fed the bond market $10 billion of new 30-year bonds on Thursday. Earlier in the week, the market received $16 billion in three-year notes and $12 billion in 10-year notes on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively.
Market strategists said the long-awaited 30-year auction, which posted an average yield of 6.445 percent and a stop out rate of 6.452 percent, offered some positive features.
"It had a tight tail and a good bid-to-cover ratio," said Michelle Laughlin, chief U.S. Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc.
The bellwether bond jumped 8/32 immediately after the auction results were released, but gains were cut sharply in lack of follow through buying and profit taking.

Laughlin said Friday trade should fare better in the wake of the supply. However, the upside potential will be limited as nervousness mounts ahead of the July retail sales report slated for release next Wednesday, she conceded.

Mike Cloherty, senior market economist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp, said he is calling for a 0.5 percent jump in total retail sales and about a 0.4-percent rise in sales excluding automobile sales.
"Normally when you get retail sales at 0.5 percent that would imply strong consumer demand. But given the extremely low level sales in June, a 0.5-percent increase in not very impressive," he said.

Meanwhile, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco President Robert Parry is scheduled to speak on the economy in Bellevue, Washington at 1530 EDT/1930 GMT. Also, Atlanta Federal Reserve President Jack Guynn is slated to speak at a business luncheon in West Palm Beach, Florida at 1245 EDT/1745 GMT.
Late on Thursday, the outstanding long bond was off 21/32 at 101-07/32, yielding 6.53 percent. The federal funds rate is expected to open at 5-7/16.

Reaser said she believed signs of vigor hinted at by this week's economic data may reignite expectations of a Federal Reserve interest rate move later this year. "Employment and the purchasing management index all show the economy is far from dead," she said.
Williams noted that Treasury prices have given "quite a concession today" and "the refunding next week will go OK at these levels."

Liro pointed out that next week's refunding should pick up momentum as the week progresses. So, while three-year notes may not see as lively investor interest, the 30-year bonds should be well received, he said.
